name: Machine & Deep Learning
desc: Regression, logistic, kernels/SVM, kNN, k-means, SOM, random forest, Naive Bayes, semi-supervised, unsupervised NNs, CNNs, R-CNN, YOLO, DenseNet, Deep-Q-Nets

topics.name: Linear & Multiple Linear Regression
notes: **Simple linear regression**: Y = b₀ + b₁X + ε. **Slope b₁** = change in Y for a 1-unit change in X; **intercept b₀** = Y when X = 0. Y = 55.1 + 0.28X → Y changes by 0.28 (the slope) per unit of X.
**Least squares** picks the line that **minimises the sum of squared residuals (SSE)** — that is the best-fit line. b₁ = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / Σ(x−x̄)², b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄.

**R² (coefficient of determination)** = 1 − SSE/SST = SSR/SST (0 to 1). SST = 400, SSE = 75 → R² = 0.8125. **Adjusted R²** penalises extra predictors. R² is the key metric for regression models (recall, precision and F-score are classification metrics).
**Correlation r** ∈ [−1, 1]: strong positive → close to +1, strong negative → close to −1. r² = R² in simple regression. Swapping X and Y keeps r, R² and the slope's sign but changes SSE.
**Assumptions on the error ε (LINE)**: Linearity, Independence of errors, Normality, Equal variance (homoscedasticity), and **E(ε) = 0** (NOT 1).
**Multiple linear regression**: Y = b₀ + b₁X₁ + … + bₖXₖ. Problem: **multicollinearity** (check VIF). Each coefficient is the effect holding the other variables constant.
Error metrics: **MSE, RMSE, MAE**. Gradient descent can also fit the model iteratively. Scaling the target changes the size of the residuals (and SSE).
Positive linear relationship: Y increases as X increases (upward slope). Negative: Y decreases as X increases.

topics.name: Logistic Regression
notes: **Logistic regression** = **classification** (binary: pass/fail, fire/no fire). Output P(Y=1) = **σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^−z)**, z = b₀ + b₁x₁ + …. σ(0) = 0.5.
**Odds** = P / (1 − P) = probability the event happens ÷ probability it doesn't. P = 0.75 → odds = 0.75/0.25 = **3**. **Log-odds (logit)** = ln(P/(1−P)) is linear in the inputs.
The coefficient bᵢ changes the log-odds by bᵢ per unit of xᵢ; **e^bᵢ = odds ratio**.
Trained by **maximum likelihood**, i.e. minimising **log loss / binary cross-entropy** (not SSE). Decision threshold usually 0.5.
Multi-class → **softmax (multinomial) regression** or one-vs-rest.
Classification metrics: accuracy, **precision = TP/(TP+FP)**, **recall = TP/(TP+FN)**, F1 = 2PR/(P+R), confusion matrix, ROC-AUC.

topics.name: Linear vs Non-linear Models & Kernel Functions
notes: **Linearly separable** data can be split by a straight line/hyperplane. **XOR** is the classic non-linearly-separable problem (a single perceptron can't learn it).
**SVM** finds the **maximum-margin hyperplane** w·x + b = 0; margin = 2/‖w‖. Points on the margin are **support vectors** (only they define the boundary).
**Hard margin**: no misclassification (separable data). **Soft margin**: slack variables; **C** large → narrow margin, low bias / high variance; C small → wide margin, more regularisation.

**Kernel trick**: compute inner products in a high-dimensional feature space without mapping explicitly: K(x, y) = φ(x)·φ(y). Kernels must be symmetric positive semi-definite (**Mercer's condition**).
Common kernels: **Linear** x·y; **Polynomial** (x·y + c)^d; **RBF/Gaussian** exp(−γ‖x − y‖²) (infinite-dimensional; large γ → wiggly boundary/overfit); **Sigmoid** tanh(αx·y + c).
Non-linear models: polynomial regression, kernel SVM, decision trees, kNN, neural networks.

topics.name: K-Nearest Neighbours
notes: **kNN** is **lazy** (no training phase; it stores the data and computes at query time), **instance-based** and **non-parametric** (makes **no assumption** about the data distribution). Used for **classification AND regression** (and for **imputing missing values**).
Prediction: find the k nearest training points → classification = **most frequent class (majority vote)**; regression = mean of the neighbours' values.
Distances: **Euclidean** √Σ(xᵢ−yᵢ)², **Manhattan** Σ|xᵢ−yᵢ|, Minkowski (generalises both), **Hamming** for **categorical** data (count of mismatches), cosine for text.

**Small k → low bias, high variance** (overfits, noisy boundary). **Large k → higher bias, lower variance, smoother boundary**. Noisy data → **increase k**. Use odd k for binary problems to avoid ties.
kNN suffers from the **curse of dimensionality** (more irrelevant attributes can hurt accuracy) and needs **feature scaling**.
Choose k with cross-validation. Common rule of thumb: k ≈ √n.

topics.name: K-means & Other Clustering Methods
notes: **K-means**: choose k centroids → assign each point to the **nearest centroid** → recompute centroids as cluster means → repeat until stable. Minimises the **within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS/inertia)**.
Choosing k: **Elbow method** (plot WCSS vs k, pick the bend) or silhouette score.

K-means weaknesses: **sensitive to outliers** and initialisation (different starts → different results; use **k-means++**), assumes convex/spherical clusters (can't find non-convex shapes), k must be given. It scales well to high-dimensional data.
**K-modes** = k-means for **categorical** data (uses modes and mismatch distance). **K-medoids** (PAM) uses actual points — more robust to outliers.
**Hierarchical (agglomerative)**: start with single points, repeatedly merge the closest clusters → dendrogram. Linkage: **single = min distance**, **complete = max distance**, average, Ward.
**DBSCAN** (density-based): eps + minPts; finds arbitrary shapes and labels noise; no k needed.
If two variables are perfectly correlated (r = 1), all points lie on a line, so the **centroids lie on a straight line** too.

topics.name: Self-Organizing Maps (Kohonen)
notes: **SOM (Kohonen map)** = an **unsupervised neural network** using **competitive learning** that maps high-dimensional data onto a low-dimensional (usually 2-D) grid while **preserving topology** (similar inputs → nearby nodes).

Algorithm: define the grid of nodes (neurons) → **initialise weight vectors randomly** → for each input, find the **Best Matching Unit (BMU)** = node with the closest weight → update **the BMU and its neighbours** towards the input → shrink the neighbourhood radius and learning rate over time.
Update rule: w(t+1) = w(t) + η(t)·h(BMU, i, t)·(x − w(t)). h is the neighbourhood function (often Gaussian).

Clustering with SOMs is in principle **similar to k-means** (prototypes move toward data), but neighbours are also updated, giving an ordered map. Used for visualisation, clustering and dimensionality reduction.
SOMs have **no backpropagation** and no target outputs.

topics.name: Decision Trees, Random Forest, Bagging & Boosting
notes: **Decision tree** splits on features to maximise purity. Impurity: **Entropy** H = −Σp log₂p (max 1 for a 50/50 binary split), **Gini** = 1 − Σp² (0.5 for 50/50). **Information gain** = parent entropy − weighted child entropy (ID3/C4.5); CART uses Gini.
Trees overfit easily (high variance) → pruning, max depth, or ensembles.
**Bagging (bootstrap aggregating)**: train models on **random samples drawn with replacement**, then average/vote → **reduces variance** (not bias).

**Random Forest** = bagging of decision trees + a **random subset of features at each split** (≈ √p for classification) → decorrelated trees. Gives an out-of-bag (OOB) error estimate and feature importance.
**Boosting** (AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost): train learners **sequentially**, each focusing on previous errors → **reduces bias**.

**AdaBoost**: learner weight α = ½ ln((1 − ε)/ε); points **misclassified by the round-t learner get higher weight** in round t + 1. Learners with error > 0.5 would get **negative α** (useless for voting), so they are discarded or flipped.

topics.name: Naive Bayes Classifier
notes: **Bayes' theorem**: P(Y|X) = P(X|Y)·P(Y) / P(X). Naive Bayes picks the class with the largest P(Y)·Π P(xᵢ|Y).
**Naive assumption**: features are **conditionally independent given the class**.
Parameters for n Boolean features + Boolean label: P(Y = 1) (1) + P(xᵢ = 1 | Y = y) for each i and both y values (2n) → **2n + 1**. With 4 inputs → 9.
Even with infinite data satisfying its assumptions, NB is only **Bayes-optimal**, so it **may still have non-zero training and test error** (classes can overlap).
Variants: **Gaussian NB** (continuous), **Multinomial NB** (word counts — text/spam), **Bernoulli NB** (binary features). **Laplace (add-1) smoothing** avoids zero probabilities.
Fast, works with little data, great for text classification; it is a **generative** model.

topics.name: Semi-Supervised Learning & EM
notes: **Semi-supervised learning** uses a **small amount of labelled data + a large amount of unlabelled data** (labels are expensive, raw data is cheap).

Methods: **self-training** (train → pseudo-label the confident unlabelled points → retrain), **co-training** (two views/classifiers label data for each other), **label propagation** on graphs, semi-supervised SVM (TSVM), generative models with **EM**.
Assumptions: **smoothness**, **cluster** (points in the same cluster share a label), **manifold** (data lies on a low-dimensional manifold).
**Transductive** = label only the given unlabelled points; **inductive** = learn a general model.

**EM algorithm** (latent variables): **E-step** computes the expected values/posteriors of the latent variables; **M-step** maximises the expected log-likelihood. For **MAP** estimates, add the log-prior in the **M-step**.

topics.name: Unsupervised Training of Neural Networks
notes: **Autoencoder**: encoder compresses the input into a **bottleneck (latent code)**; the decoder reconstructs it; trained to **minimise reconstruction error** (input = target) → unsupervised feature learning, dimensionality reduction, denoising (denoising AE), anomaly detection.

**Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM)**: visible + hidden layers, no intra-layer connections; trained with **contrastive divergence**. Stacked RBMs → **Deep Belief Network** (greedy layer-wise pre-training).
**Hebbian learning**: "neurons that fire together wire together" — Δw = η·x·y. **Competitive learning**: winner-take-all (basis of SOM).
**Greedy layer-wise unsupervised pre-training** initialises deep nets one layer at a time, then fine-tunes with supervision.
**GANs**: generator vs discriminator trained adversarially (generative modelling). **Variational autoencoders** learn a probabilistic latent space.
Backprop basics: gradients through **sigmoid/tanh are multiplied by positive derivatives**, so they **cannot change sign** — but they shrink (σ' ≤ 0.25) → **vanishing gradients**. ReLU helps.

topics.name: CNN Architectures
notes: **Convolution layer**: filters slide over the input; output size = **(W − F + 2P)/S + 1** (W input, F filter, P padding, S stride). Parameters per layer = **(F × F × C_in + 1) × K** filters (shared weights → far fewer parameters than dense layers).
**Pooling** (max/average) downsamples (2 × 2, stride 2 halves width and height) → translation invariance, fewer computations. ReLU adds non-linearity. Fully connected layers + softmax classify.
**LeNet-5** (LeCun, 1998): handwritten digits, 32 × 32 input, conv–pool–conv–pool–FC.
**AlexNet** (2012, ImageNet winner): 5 conv + 3 FC, **ReLU, dropout, data augmentation, GPUs**; 227 × 227 input, first layer 96 filters 11 × 11 stride 4 → 55 × 55; ~60M parameters.
**VGG-16/19** (2014): only **3 × 3 convolutions** stacked deep; ~138M parameters (simple but heavy).

**GoogLeNet / Inception v1** (2014): **Inception modules** with parallel 1×1, 3×3, 5×5 convs + pooling; **1 × 1 convolutions** reduce depth (bottleneck); 22 layers, ~5M parameters; global average pooling.
**ResNet** (2015): **residual/skip connections** y = F(x) + x (addition) let very deep nets (50/101/152 layers) train — fixes degradation/vanishing gradients.
**Dropout** randomly drops neurons during training (regularisation). **Batch normalisation** normalises layer inputs → faster, stabler training. **Transfer learning**: reuse pretrained CNN features.

topics.name: R-CNN, Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN & Mask R-CNN
notes: **Object detection** = classify objects **and** localise them with bounding boxes. Quality is measured with **IoU** (intersection / union of boxes) and **mAP**.

**R-CNN** (Girshick, 2014): **selective search → ~2000 region proposals** → warp each region → CNN features (AlexNet) → **class-specific SVMs** + **bounding-box regression**. Accurate but **very slow** (a CNN pass per region), multi-stage training.

**Fast R-CNN** (2015): run the CNN **once on the whole image** → **RoI pooling** extracts a fixed-size feature map per proposal → softmax classifier + box regressor trained jointly (multi-task loss). Still uses selective search.
**Faster R-CNN** (2015): replaces selective search with a **Region Proposal Network (RPN)** that shares conv features and uses **anchor boxes** → nearly real-time, end-to-end.
**Mask R-CNN** (2017): Faster R-CNN + a **mask branch** for **instance segmentation**; uses **RoIAlign** instead of RoI pooling.
R-CNN family = **two-stage detectors** (propose, then classify). YOLO/SSD = one-stage. **Non-max suppression (NMS)** removes duplicate boxes.

topics.name: YOLO (You Only Look Once)
notes: **YOLO** (Redmon et al., 2016) treats detection as a **single regression problem**: one CNN pass predicts boxes and class probabilities directly → a **one-stage detector**, **real-time** (~45 fps; Fast YOLO ~155 fps).

YOLO v1 divides the image into an **S × S grid (7 × 7)**. Each cell predicts **B = 2 boxes** (x, y, w, h, confidence) and **C class probabilities** → output **S × S × (B·5 + C) = 7 × 7 × 30** for PASCAL VOC (C = 20).
**Confidence** = P(object) × IoU(pred, truth). The cell containing an object's **centre** is responsible for it.
Strengths: very fast, sees the whole image (fewer background errors). Weaknesses (v1): **small objects in groups**, unusual aspect ratios, poorer localisation.
**YOLOv2** added **anchor boxes** and batch norm; **YOLOv3** uses **Darknet-53** and predicts at **3 scales**. NMS removes duplicates.

topics.name: DenseNet
notes: **DenseNet** (Huang et al., 2017): within a **dense block**, **each layer receives the feature maps of ALL preceding layers** (connected by **concatenation**, not addition) and passes its own maps to all later layers.
A dense block with L layers has **L(L + 1)/2 direct connections**.
**Growth rate k** = number of feature maps each layer adds. The l-th layer has k₀ + k(l − 1) input channels; a block with L layers outputs k₀ + L·k channels.
**Transition layers** between blocks: BN → **1 × 1 conv** → **2 × 2 average pooling** (reduce size and channels; compression factor θ).
**DenseNet-B** uses 1 × 1 bottleneck convs; **DenseNet-BC** = bottleneck + compression. Common models: DenseNet-121/169/201.
Benefits: **feature reuse**, **alleviates vanishing gradients**, strong gradient flow, **fewer parameters** than ResNet for similar accuracy, regularising effect.
**ResNet adds** (x + F(x)); **DenseNet concatenates** [x₀, x₁, …, x_{l−1}].

topics.name: Reinforcement Learning & Deep-Q-Networks
notes: **RL**: an agent takes actions in states, receives **rewards**, and aims to maximise the **discounted return** G = r₁ + γr₂ + γ²r₃ + … (0 ≤ γ < 1).
**Q(s, a)** = expected return from taking action a in state s and then acting optimally. **Bellman optimality**: Q*(s, a) = E[r + γ max_a' Q*(s', a')].

**Q-learning** (off-policy, model-free): Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α [r + γ max_a' Q(s', a') − Q(s, a)] → converges to the **optimal policy** (π* = argmax Q). TD(0)/TD(1)/direct evaluation only estimate V(s) for a fixed policy. **SARSA** is on-policy.
**Deep Q-Network (DQN)** (DeepMind, Mnih et al. 2013/2015): a **CNN approximates Q(s, a)** from raw pixels (Atari games), outputting a Q-value for each action.

DQN stabilisers: **experience replay** (store transitions, sample random mini-batches → breaks correlations) and a **target network** (a periodically copied network that computes the targets r + γ max Q_target(s', a')).

Exploration: **ε-greedy** (random action with probability ε, decayed over time). Improvements: **Double DQN** (reduces overestimation), **Dueling DQN** (separate V(s) and advantage A(s, a)), prioritised replay.
